What is jQuery and why was it so popular?

A fast, small JS library (about 30 KB gzipped) that gave one consistent API across browsers at a time when IE6–8, Firefox and Safari all behaved differently. Its strengths: CSS-selector DOM queries, implicit iteration and chaining, easy event handling, a simple AJAX API, animations, and a huge plugin ecosystem (DataTables, Select2, jQuery Validation).
$(document).ready() vs window.onload?

ready fires when the DOM is parsed (DOMContentLoaded), before images and stylesheets finish loading. You can register many handlers, and they still run if registered after the event has fired. window.onload waits for everything (images, CSS, iframes), and assigning it directly allows only one handler (each assignment overwrites the last). Use ready for DOM setup and load when you need image dimensions.
What does $ mean? What is jQuery.noConflict()?

$ is just an alias for the jQuery function. If another library (Prototype, an old MooTools) also uses $, call jQuery.noConflict() to release it, then use jQuery(...) or wrap your code: (function($){ ... })(jQuery);.
.attr() vs .prop()?

.attr() reads and writes the HTML attribute, which is the initial value in the markup. .prop() reads and writes the live DOM property, which is the current state. For checkboxes, .attr('checked') keeps returning the original attribute after the user clicks, while .prop('checked') returns true or false. Use prop for checked, selected, disabled and value-like state, and attr for things like href, data-* and aria-*.
.text() vs .html() vs .val()?

.text() gets or sets text content and escapes HTML, so it's XSS-safe. .html() gets or sets inner HTML and parses markup, so it's dangerous with user input. .val() gets or sets the value of form controls (input, select, textarea).
.on() vs .click() vs .bind()/.live()/.delegate()?

.on() (since 1.7) is the single unified API. .click(fn) is shorthand for .on('click', fn). .bind() and .delegate() are deprecated and .live() was removed, all in favour of .on(). With a selector argument, .on('click', '.row', fn) does delegation: the handler sits on the parent and matches descendants, including ones added later. Remove handlers with .off(), and use namespaces ('click.myPlugin') so you can remove only your own.
event.preventDefault() vs event.stopPropagation() vs return false?

preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form). stopPropagation() stops the event bubbling up to ancestors. return false in a jQuery handler does both. In a native addEventListener handler it does neither, and in an inline onclick attribute it only prevents the default. Be explicit and call the methods you mean.
.remove() vs .detach() vs .empty()?

.empty() removes the children but keeps the element. .remove() removes the element and its jQuery data and event handlers. .detach() removes the element but keeps its data and events, so you can re-insert it later (useful for heavy DOM manipulation off-screen).
this vs $(this) inside a handler?

this is the raw DOM element, so you use native APIs like this.value and this.id. $(this) wraps it in a jQuery object so you can use .closest(), .data() and so on. In arrow functions this isn't the element, so use e.currentTarget. Cache wrappers you use repeatedly: const $btn = $(this);.
What is a Deferred / Promise in jQuery? $.when?

$.Deferred() is jQuery's promise implementation. You resolve or reject it, and consumers chain .done(), .fail(), .always() and .then(). Every $.ajax call returns a jqXHR, which is a Deferred, so $.when(a, b).done(...) waits for several requests in parallel, like Promise.all. Since jQuery 3, Deferreds follow Promises/A+ and work with await.
What does .serialize() do? How do you send JSON instead?

$('form').serialize() produces a URL-encoded string (name=Arun&age=30), which Spring binds with @ModelAttribute or @RequestParam. .serializeArray() gives [{name, value}]. For a @RequestBody JSON endpoint, build an object and send JSON.stringify(obj) with contentType: 'application/json'.
How do you improve jQuery performance?

Cache selectors (const $list = $('#list')). Start from an ID and use .find() rather than broad selectors. Build HTML in memory and insert it once instead of appending in a loop. Use event delegation instead of thousands of handlers. Detach elements before heavy changes. Avoid jQuery-only pseudo-selectors (:visible, :first) in hot paths, and prefer CSS animations. Or replace jQuery with native APIs.
.closest() vs .parents() vs .parent()?

.parent() goes up exactly one level. .parents(sel) returns all matching ancestors up to the document. .closest(sel) starts with the element itself and returns the first match going up (zero or one element), which makes it the standard choice for finding the row from a clicked button.
Should you use jQuery with Angular?

Generally no. Angular owns the DOM through templates and change detection, and jQuery changes are invisible to it, which causes inconsistent state, memory leaks and SSR problems. Use bindings, directives, Renderer2, or ElementRef sparingly. If a legacy jQuery plugin is unavoidable, wrap it in a directive: initialize it in ngAfterViewInit, destroy it in ngOnDestroy, and run it outside the Angular zone if it's noisy.
What does .data('id', 5) do to the DOM attribute?

Nothing. It writes to jQuery's internal cache only. .data('id') returns 5, but .attr('data-id') gives the old value, and a selector [data-id="5"] does not match. To keep them in sync, use .attr('data-id', 5). Note that after .data() has cached the value, later .attr() changes are not seen by .data().
Why does $('#a').map(...) not behave like an array, and how do you fix it?

jQuery's .map returns a jQuery object, with an argument order of (index, element), the reverse of Array.prototype.map. Call .get() or .toArray() for a real array. $.map(array, (value, index) => ...) is different again: the order is (value, index), and returned arrays are flattened, while null results are removed.
Why is a delegated handler sometimes not firing?

- An inner handler calls stopPropagation(), so the event never reaches the delegating ancestor.
- The ancestor itself was replaced, for instance by .html() on the parent, which removes the listener.
- The event does not bubble natively. jQuery maps focus and blur to bubbling versions for delegation.
- The selector does not match at click time. It is evaluated against the element and its ancestors up to the delegate.
$(el).remove() vs el.remove(): why does it matter for memory?

jQuery stores handlers and data in its own internal structure, linked to the element. $(el).remove(), .empty() and .html('...') clean up that data for the removed subtree. Native el.remove() or el.innerHTML = '' leaves the entries behind, so handler closures stay referenced, a slow leak. In a page that mixes both, always remove through jQuery.
.prop('disabled') vs .attr('disabled') vs .is(':disabled'); how do you read a checkbox?

.prop('checked') returns a boolean for the current state, and .is(':checked') gives the same result as a readable test. .attr('checked') reflects the markup, returning 'checked' or undefined, and does not follow clicks. For all checked values in a group: $('input[name=role]:checked').map((i, e) => e.value).get(). .val() on a checkbox gives its value attribute, not whether it is checked.
What's the cost of :visible, :first and other jQuery extensions?

jQuery first tries the fast native querySelectorAll. Pseudo-selectors that are not CSS, such as :first, :eq(), :visible and :has() (in older browsers), make it fall back to the slower Sizzle engine in JavaScript. :visible also reads layout, forcing a reflow per element. Use .filter(':visible') on a small set, and .first() instead of :first.
Why is async: false a bad idea? What does it do to the page?

It makes a synchronous XHR, freezing the main thread, so that clicks, scroll and animation all stop until the response arrives. Synchronous XHR on the main thread is deprecated, and browsers log a warning. It also cannot be used with dataType: 'jsonp'. Developers use it to "return" a value from a function. The fix is to return the jqXHR or a promise and to continue in .done() or with await.
What's the output order? $(fn) vs inline code, and .then on a resolved Deferred in jQuery 3.
How do you migrate a jQuery page to modern code step by step?

- Upgrade to the latest 3.x with jQuery Migrate, and fix its warnings.
- Put tests around key flows with Playwright or Cypress.
- Replace helpers with native equivalents (fetch, classList, closest), starting with new code.
- Replace plugins one at a time. DataTables and Select2 have non-jQuery options.
- Rewrite heavy screens as Angular components or web components, mounted inside the old page, and move routes over gradually (the strangler pattern).
- Remove jQuery when no code uses it. Some plugins keep it alive for a long time, so track these.

$.extend shallow vs deep; how is it different from spread?

$.extend({}, a, b) copies top-level properties, like { ...a, ...b }. $.extend(true, {}, a, b) merges recursively into plain objects and arrays. Two differences from spread: $.extend skips undefined values, while spread copies them; and it also copies inherited enumerable properties. Calling it without a target object as first argument modifies the first object, a frequent bug when defaults gets changed for all calls.

Why does Spring not bind an array sent with $.ajax data: { ids: [1, 2] }?

By default $.param serializes arrays in PHP style as ids[]=1&ids[]=2, and Spring's @RequestParam List<Long> ids expects ids=1&ids=2. Pass traditional: true in the $.ajax options (or set it in $.ajaxSetup), or send JSON with contentType: 'application/json' and JSON.stringify to a @RequestBody.
$.each vs .each: what is the difference?

$('li').each(fn) iterates over a jQuery collection of DOM elements; inside, this is the raw element. $.each(obj, fn) is a general utility that iterates over any array or object; the callback gets (index, value) or (key, value). In both, returning false stops the loop early, which native forEach cannot do. Note the argument order is the reverse of native forEach(value, index).
What changed in jQuery 4, and what breaks when upgrading?

jQuery 4 drops support for old browsers such as IE 10 and earlier, removes long-deprecated utilities (for example $.isArray, $.trim, $.type, $.isFunction, $.now; use native equivalents), and changes some focus event ordering and JSONP auto-promotion behaviour. The safe path is: upgrade to the latest 3.x, add jQuery Migrate to log every deprecated call, fix the warnings, then move to 4 and remove Migrate. Check that plugins such as DataTables or Select2 support the target version.
$.ajax vs $.get / $.post vs $.getJSON vs .load(): which do you use?

| $.ajax | $.get / $.post | $.getJSON | .load()
What it is | The full API | Shorthand for GET / POST | GET with dataType 'json' | GET HTML into selected elements
Headers, timeout, contentType | All options | Only url, data, success, dataType | Only url, data, success | Only url, data, complete
Send a JSON body | Yes (contentType + JSON.stringify) | No, form-encoded by default | No | No
Returns | jqXHR (a promise) | jqXHR | jqXHR | The jQuery object (chainable)
Typical use | REST calls to Spring | Quick form-style calls | Simple read-only JSON | Inject a server-rendered fragment
$.ajax({ url: '/api/patients', method: 'POST',
  contentType: 'application/json', data: JSON.stringify(p) })
 .done(saved => render(saved))
 .fail(xhr => showError(xhr.status));
Rule of thumb: use $.ajax for any call to a @RequestBody endpoint; the shorthands only save typing for simple GETs and form posts.
.done / .fail / .always vs .then vs the old success / error callbacks?

| success / error options | .done / .fail / .always | .then(ok, fail)
Where you write it | Inside the options object | Chained on the jqXHR | Chained on the jqXHR
Several handlers | One each | As many as you like | As many as you like
Return value | Ignored | Same promise (no transform) | New promise with the returned value
Chain dependent calls | Nesting (callback hell) | Awkward | Yes, return the next request
Status | Still works | Still works | Promises/A+ compatible since jQuery 3
Rule of thumb: use .done/.fail for side effects, and .then when one call needs the result of the previous one. .always is the place to hide a spinner.
.append() vs .prepend() vs .after() vs .before() vs .html()?

Method | Where the new content goes | Existing content
.append(x) | Inside, as the last child | Kept
.prepend(x) | Inside, as the first child | Kept
.after(x) | Outside, as the next sibling | Kept
.before(x) | Outside, as the previous sibling | Kept
.html(x) | Inside, replacing all children | Removed (and its jQuery data and handlers cleaned)
Interview tip: .appendTo(), .prependTo(), .insertAfter() and .insertBefore() do the same with source and target swapped. Passing a string containing user data to any of them parses it as HTML, so build elements with .text() instead to avoid XSS.
.find() vs .children() vs .filter() vs .is()?

| .find(sel) | .children(sel) | .filter(sel) | .is(sel)
Searches | All descendants | Direct children only | The current set itself | The current set itself
Returns | New jQuery set | New jQuery set | Subset of the current set | Boolean
Selector required | Yes | No (all children) | Yes (or a function) | Yes (or a function)
Example | $('form').find('input') | $('ul').children('.active') | $('tr').filter('.selected') | $(this).is(':checked')
Rule of thumb: .find and .children move down the tree, .filter narrows what you already have, and .is just answers yes or no.
